I owned a retail copy of Strife. I consider myself fortunate to have enjoyed the game when it spearheaded the inclusion of RPG elements, player-controlled speech, and story-driven missions into the still relatively young genre of first person shooters. That being said, I think it can be difficult for people who got into gaming after Deus Ex popularized those things to appreciate how experimental and innovative Strife was for its time.

Strife wasn't just a marvel in video game design; it presented its players with fun and challenging action, and a compelling narrative. Those things still hold up well to this day, and so I was intrigued when I learned that Nightdive Studios had remastered the game and published a "Veteran Edition" of it.

When Strife had initially been published in 1996, it looked dated because it was built atop id Software's Doom engine. Quake was id Software's next title, and it was set to be published about one month after Strife hit shelves. It was obvious that Quake was about to take visuals in first person shooters to a whole new level. The previews that were available to the public regarding Quake's appearance and its polygon-based 3D engine likely overshadowed the attention that Strife would have otherwise attracted. Strife managed to gain a small cult following, but myself and much of the gaming press contend that it deserved a lot more sales and fame than it received.

When playing the Veteran Edition of Strife, the game retains an aesthetic that makes it simultaneously appear dated yet intriguingly distinct. Nightdive has given players access to many visual and auditory options that they can natively enable or disable, as well as modern keyboard controls and mouselook functionality. These improvements don't just make the game super accessible to modern gamers; they completely eliminate the need to run Strife through source ports. Strife now looks better than ever before, with bright colors, improved lighting, and overblown gore effects that I found quite startling - even when compared to games as over the top as Rise of The Triad.

From what I understand, a multiplayer mode had been planned for Strife, but never ended up getting patched into the original game. Although I am pleased to report that Nightdive has added it to the Veteran Edition, I can't speak to its quality. That's because I've never been able to find another player since I tried to take the game online in 2025. In spite of that, I feel pleased knowing that the potential to easily take Strife online exists thanks to the native matchmaking that exists in the Veteran Edition.

Strife's single player campaign has also been expanded upon a little bit. There isn't a lot of new content, but I really appreciate what was added. These new areas and challenges made Strife: Veteran Edition a joy to play more than a decade since I last experienced - and beat - the original version of Strife. I ended up discovering things that seemed completely new to me, but that might have everything to do with me having forgotten about them.

One thing that set Strife apart from all the other games that had been based on the Doom engine is its heavy emphasis on story, with new missions unfolding during game play. Many of those missions depend upon crucial decisions that the player makes within the game - either through his/her words or actions. The Veteran edition is true to the original by preserving those things. However, it mercifully gives players the change to fight their way out of a predicament they can put themselves into early in the game. It is quite possible that some players gave up on Strife because of it, being frustrated that the game 'allowed' them to get themselves into an inescapable situation. (In defense of how the game had originally been designed, the game's motto is "Trust no one", and the situation I referenced is one that reinforces that motto.)

Strife's music is serviceable. It's nothing to write home about, nor it is terrible. As with other remasters designed by Nightdive Studios, you have the choice of listening to an arranged rendition of the original tunes. The game's sound effects and voice acting are unchanged, but I think most players will be very happy with that - as both of those things are excellent, even by modern standards. The only exception I can think of are the Templars, which have a habit of repeating a noise that is as obnoxious as it is robotic. I suppose Nightdive could have added voice acting for inconsequential non-player characters, but I'm not going to hold the absence of that against the company or this product.

Should you play Strife: Veteran Edition? If you like first person shooters, I'd say you'll likely enjoy this title. It feels distinctly old school, yet is simultaneously quite different from the vast majority of first person shooters from the 90s. You won't get far trying to use violence against everyone and everything you meet, and succumbing to a desire for violence and aggression means you likely won't be able to appreciate the plot and how it is central to the places you can go.

If you're someone who likes a good combination of combat, exploration, and critical thinking, I think you may enjoy this game. Even if you played the original version of Strife, like I did, I still recommend playing Strife: Veteran Edition. If you enjoyed the original and haven't played it a while, I bet you'll like the Veteran Edition at least as much as the original - if not a fair bit more.

Easily my favourite retro game, and I say that knowing all the classics by ID, Apogee and 3DRealms through and through. It has everything it possibly could - enthralling setting (techno-fantasy postapocalypse with guns, castles and cyborg templars as your enemies - could it ever get more awesome?!) great story (there are some illusoric choices - that's bad, but forgiveable - and some that can block the way for you, which is actually brilliant. No modern game ever did that!), a wide array of cool guns to put your hands on, multiple endings... 

And a really, really sexy sidekick. Yeah, she's just a voice in your comm, but man, what a voice it is!

Weapons you get seem gimmicky - among which there's an assault rifle that is a good all-rounder but rips through your ammo reserves like crazy, a plasma shotgun which is cool but even worse in this aspect, a grenade launcher that is really easy to blow yourself up with, a psionic relic that shoots thunder and lightning at the expense of your own health (and gets more and more powerful with each big bad you murder)... And a dagger that in your capable hands is able to turn enemies into red mist. All of these require careful inventory management and take some actual skill to aim and fire. 

Managing your health is even more important - you can buy more medical supplies for gold, but there's never enough of both. All in all, on higher difficulty levels Strife really offers a challenge.

It's a pseudo-open world - sort of, as locations are opened to you one by one as story progresses. You are able to revisit, and some of the levels are purely optional. By the end, the game does get a little crazy with numbers of enemies set against you which seems a bit tedious, but the story is about enough compelling to keep you moving forward.

Strife was way ahead of its time, but went through in the shadow of other, louder titles, despite being so much better than most of them. It just isn't right to leave it here, forgotten, unknown. If you enjoy old school FPSes, you simply cannot pass on this one.

There is a term, used for platformers mainly, 'Metroidvania'. It is the result of the games Metroid and Castlevania, that had such impact in the game development, that are used as examples nowadays. Strife is to the FPS-RPG genre what Metroid and Castlevania are to platformers.

It is one of the best titles made on doom engine and it was the first that combined RPG elements to a FPS game, by inserting NPCs, quests and voiced dialogues! A part of gaming history, remade on December 2014, 18 years later than its original release. Strife is a first person shooter with some role playing elements, such as quests, talking with NPCs and some decision making that may, or may not, have direct effect to your gameplay! [spoiler alert: there are 3 endings!]

Truly a hidden gem and a must play for every Doom/Quake/Hexen and even DeusEx (the first) lover. It can be as difficult and demanding as you want it to be with since the Veteran Edition has kept all the features of the Original, difficulty levels included! You can also play the game as its original version (some 'vanilla' bugs are included) or the newer version that has some extras, with or without the newer graphics.

The story goes that after a meteor crashed on the planet and killed thousands, it spread a virus where the affected got mad by hearing a voice and called themselves 'the order'. Those who could not hear the voice where used as slaves or even guinea pigs, as a result a rebel movement is forged, 'the front', to fight the order. You are a mercenary that gets captured by the order and gets involved with the front. The world, while not extremely huge, may still surprise you given that there are a lot hidden items in seemingly empty areas or even hidden rooms, and a lot of different paths or backdoors in the various levels for you to explore! It also requires some thinking in addition of the mindless killing of baddies! For example: a friendly NPC tells me that in X room there are weapons, but the room is locked. The quest continues and after a while I meet an NPC that mentions that he had just finished stocking some weapons. So.... killing the NPC did gave me the key I needed!

The only negatives are, the aiming in regards to different levels (higher/lower) that can be clunky even with the games aim assist, few voice dialogues that do not have subtitle support but are quite easy to understand if you pay attention, and the graphics. Now I did not play this game for its graphics and frankly I like this retro-style a lot more than fully 3D games, but the issue is that on first sight the game is a brick of mud, that once you wash it, the gold sparkles! So sadly, it may not receive the attention it deserves.

I usually don't rate games because I find it hard to evaluate stuff like graphics, however, given that graphics here are not in the question I give this jewel, a solid 10 out of 10 just because it managed to entertain me the entire time I was playing it!

[h1] Strife: Veteran Edition! [/h1]
This old classic from 1996 often gets shadowed over from other similar games like Doom, Shadow Warrior, Blood etc.
But what separates Strife from said games, is its RPG-like elements mixed up with a 90's classic shooter creating a unique hybrid of a game. [spoiler]Though don't expect Fallout 1-like RPG elements, but I will admit it's still pretty unique that it manages to fuse together a 90's shooter with RPG. [/spoiler]

[h1] The Story [/h1]
Now, in most old school classic games, the story is either nothing complex or is usually unimportant.
But in Strife, [spoiler] A comet strikes your planet, releasing a virus within. Which decimates human civilization, and henceforth creates The Order. However a group of humans create The Front and try their best to fight The Order, that's when you; Strifeguy/Mercenary decided to work for The Front, before being caught and executed by The Order, but luckily for you....[/spoiler]

[h1] The Gameplay [/h1]
If you have played Hexen 1 before, then you might have an idea of how the gameplay mostly plays out.
So, the game is home to a massive hub level called the Town and from here you can access different maps like the Sewers, the Prison, the Power Station and so on. Later on you access the Borderlands and Order Commons which unlock more and harder levels.
Another thing worth mentioning is that, unlike other Doom-like games. In Strife, you talk and interact with characters to complete quests and progress the story or buying armor, ammo, weapons, medkits or even miscellaneous items.

[h1] The Music [/h1]
The music is all composed by someone named Morey Goldstein. [spoiler]heh[/spoiler] You will be hearing from 90's music all the way to more sinister pieces.

[h1] The Weapons [/h1]
The Mercenary has a huge array of weapons to choose from. The Punch Dagger all the way to the Sigil, which absorbs the player's health but deals massive damage. Some weapons like the crossbow and the grenade launcher allow the player to use different ammunition suited for different situations.

[h1] Level Design/ Setting [/h1]
A huge problem that old 90's shooters had was that you could get stuck very easily in a level trying to find a switch or finding an exit. But Strife has an automap which helps a lot if you happen to get stuck but even without the map I always managed to find my path, thanks to the suburb level design the game has. However, there are areas like the Sewers and to a lesser degree the Catacombs where players can get stuck. (myself included)
The setting is like this medieval like setting along with advanced technology, however as weird as it sounds it blends in SUPER well so it never really sticks out or anything like that.

[h1] Achievements [/h1]
For those who care, the game comes with 20 unique achievements!
19 of which are singleplayer and only 1 being multiplayer.
Some are obtained normally while you progress, for others you have to look into secret areas  or play harder difficulties.

[h1] Final Verdict [/h1]
If you are someone who loves classic 90's shooters then having this game is a must-have because it is a CRIMINALLY underrated game.
My only gripes with the game is towards the end levels, i.e The Factory levels where you encounter powerful enemy waves after waves and in bloodbath difficulty they keep respawning. You can imagine how fun that is.
But if you can look past that, this is a really fun experience.

[spoiler]And my only true supper gripe I had is that this game never had a sequel. A game this awesome DESERVES a sequel.[/spoiler]

Strife is the result of the enormous influence that Doom had in its time, leading to the market invasion by myriad "clones" of it, the so-called Doom-likes, but when we talk about Strife, we don't have a normal first-person shooter in our hands.

Strife is one of the first video games to propose a shooter experience combined with role-playing game elements, much like Deus Ex, for instance.

The game takes us to a world that is somewhat futuristic-medieval, which, at certain points, reminds one of Star Wars, in an atmosphere characterized by a typical post-apocalyptic situation where humans find themselves facing invaders ready to reshape and subjugate them.

Our character will be a typical silent protagonist whose face will be visible only in some illustrations that serve as cutscenes. We play as an adventurer who becomes the ace up the sleeve of the rebellion in overturning the invaders' order.

The RPG elements of the game are felt right from the beginning, especially when looking at the weapons, whose characteristics have been directly influenced by this component.

The first weapon is a simple blade (similar to Assassin's Creed), the only melee weapon in the game that allows us, optionally, to perform stealth kills. But the real weapon that somehow represents a certain touch of originality is the crossbow, whose presence is a direct consequence of the chivalrous style that characterizes the game.

This weapon will have two types of ammunition: electric arrows, noisy and effective against any type of enemy, and poisoned arrows, lethal with a single shot, effective only against human enemies, and capable of stealth kills.

The other weapons are typical heavy and light weapons of the genre, with the exception of a third weapon that is directly influenced by the RPG component of the game, namely the Sigil, a powerful energy weapon that uses our protagonist's HP as ammunition, in a sense. It will be expanded and enhanced over time by collecting artifacts released by bosses, which will not only change its appearance but also the way the fired projectiles disperse, as if gradually, through upgrades, the weapon becomes more stable, concentrating all its energy into a single central shot.

Regarding the RPG aspect, it is important to highlight the existence of a leveling system, where the two parameters of stamina (character's health) and precision (accuracy of shots and damage) can be enhanced through the advice of some doctors and armorers or sometimes through interactions with certain enhancement interfaces or by overcoming challenges, such as defeating bosses or completing training in a structure.

(Curiously, just like Doom, the original version of the game didn't have the ability to use the gyroscope, which means you can't aim up or down directly with the mouse. Fortunately, this feature was introduced in the veteran edition). It's worth noting that the version I played is an enhanced one that adds several improvements to the original game, including the inventory bar. This allows us to carry a medical kit to regain health or, if desired, wear armor to reduce damage levels, unlike the good old Doom where medical kits could only be picked up from the ground.

To further discuss the RPG component, the game will present us several times with choices that, in reality, won't influence the game much except towards the end, where they could lead to two different endings, or three, if you will. Personally, I obtained a bad ending by losing against the final boss and a good ending by defeating him successfully, but I've heard that there are also partially good or partially bad endings.

In the game, it's possible to interact with some characters, and during dialogues, we will see the faces of our interlocutors on the screen, depicted with a comic style that I personally found quite enjoyable, just like the aforementioned illustrations that serve as cutscenes. Another very interesting thing, especially for its time, is the need to trust the right people because by making certain choices, you can encounter a game over from which you can't escape by fighting. These are known in visual novels as Dead-ends. It's not something avoidable with great difficulty, but it's still present.

Personally, I absolutely love the game's graphical style, which was created with ID TECH 1, the same graphic engine as the first Doom, and it's inevitable not to notice the similarities. The environment is made in 3D with polygonal models, while the characters on the screen are presented in 2D, like moving silhouettes, but in this case, they are much more detailed compared to the pixel models present in Doom.

The game features a multiplayer component, which unfortunately is difficult to access due to the lack of players on the servers, so I won't be able to judge the game as a whole. However, there is an additional mode called "Trust no one." It's not much, to be honest. It consists of the first 16 minutes of gameplay, enriched and modified in a way that the title can already suggest, and in reality, it doesn't add much to the game. Nonetheless, for those who appreciated it, it can still be 16 minutes of enjoyable alternative gameplay. If you love challenges, you could also try the challenge proposed by the game's trophies, which asks you to finish this game mode within 6 minutes in the most difficult setting.

The game's duration ranges from 10 to 15 hours. There won't be any particular approaches that will allow you to finish it faster or slower than usual, since, as I mentioned, the RPG component mainly influences the gameplay, except for a few isolated cases where, for example, it will be possible to complete a mission using a stealth approach that significantly reduces the mission's duration. However, this approach would normally require knowledge of the structure where the mission takes place, which is why I find it unlikely that a player can apply this approach in their first run.

Personally, I believe that Strife is my favorite Doom-like game. It's a classic RPG with a visual style that I particularly appreciate, just like its gameplay mechanics, and combined with its simple yet incredibly enjoyable story, it creates an unforgettable experience within the genre.

I am the sort of person who becomes incredibly enamored with 90's FPSes. Seeing my favourite genre of immersive media in its period of infancy, where the developers were still learning what works and what doesn't... There is just something magical about it, like watching old black and white movies and insisting they're better in every way to the stuff released today.

Of course they aren't. No movie buff is right when they say Kubrick's works outshine the oscarbait we get in our current decade, no photographer is right when they say pictures just look better taken with their analogue sh**boxes. We see the past with rose-tinted glasses because of many factors; nostalgia, passion, auteur admiration, but none of these make the works of the past outright better. I am saying this to quality my recommendation, because Strife was made in 1996; the games industry has had almost 20 years to innovate since this game was released, and as such, as good as the game is, is just can't outshine IPs such as half-life or the elder scrolls series.

That being said, I now feel comfortable telling you that this game is probably one of the best games I have ever played.

Strife is made on a heavily modified DOOM engine, but it plays closer to 3Drealms' Duke 3D or Shadow Warrior; you can jump, run, fill your inventory with all manner of useful gadgets, and best of all, the game contains the first example of RPG elements in an FPS game; you level up doing sidequests, you can find gold in secret areas to buy additional health packs or ammo, and the game has multiple endings based on a couple of important choices you make as a player. This sort of innovation boggles my mind for 1996, and it's even stranger to me that I had not even heard of this game until a few weeks ago.

The levels are scattered with secrets, the crux of which being 3 hidden talismans that the game makes you work like a dog for... When you finally get all three, your reward is... Well, I wont spoil it, but it was the most immensely satisfying prize you can imagine without being something inherently game ending. Strife also Gives you the option to stealth through most levels, again, one of the first FPSes that let you do this. The stealth is a little bit confusing, and isn't explained well, but hey, back in those days games came with a manual. Basically, most new areas bad guys wont consider you a threat until you open fire on them. A reasonable reaction, in my opinion. You can stop the alarms going off by killing secluded enemies with silent weapons; daggers or poison darts so that the inevitable dog-pile of enemies becomes easier to manage when they catch you being a twat. You can also... you know... just complete your objective and leave without harming anyone; an option that I doubt many people took in 1996, but an option that is mandatory for the bloodbath difficulty which is as to NIGHTMARE mode what the Holocaust is to a teletubbies marathon. Bloodbath is horrendously difficult. I can finish any level of DOOM on nightmare mode but I cant get out of the first ROOM alive on bloodbath.

The protagonist has a hardcore sidekick named blackbird who, again, in a profound innovation is the first character I have ever heard say the F-word in a video game (chronologically, I mean), which endeared her to me immediately, her ultimate role is a shoehorned love interest but hey it's the nineties, too much innovation and they would have been burned at the steak. The protagonist himself is a relatively nameless, voiceless link character who travels through 20+ levels with a stunning variety of weapons from the humble bread and butter assault rifle to the double-barreled High-Explosive grenade launcher with optional white phosphorous rounds for when you're feeling frisky. Seriously the grenade launcher is in my top 3 weapons from all games, it is an immensely satisfying, unnecessarily powerful death machine.

The bosses are good, though the only two worth mentioning are the first boss and the last boss. The first boss is a hectic fast paced battle that I barely survived, the last battle was a wonderfully cinematic ultimatum. All the other bosses get one-shot by the stupid sigil weapon (think soul cube from doom 3). This is probably the only nit-pick I have with this game. The enemies are all astounding, peons, mechs and monsters are all well-rounded and have individual character Bosses, enemies and allies are all competently voice acted, my favourite being the snarky peon administrator who just takes one look at the amount of work you went through cheating yourself into the Order's main HQ, sighs, shrugs and waves you through.

Strife is challenging, rewards exploration and proactive thinking, the levels are well designed, it has character, atmosphere, and a satisfying conclusion with loads of wonderful comic book cutscenes. From 1996, this game is exceptional, and if you adjust for inflation, it is phoenominal. If you enjoy First-person games, you OWE it to yourself to play Strife.

While this game is hailed as an FPS-RPG hybrid, I would recommend you ignore the RPG part because for the most part it's a DOOM-Clone.  If you've played games like DOOM (the Columbine shooter training simulator not the new one) or Chex Quest, this is more of the same and I'd recommend it if you've played those.  Take that previous statement with a grain of salt.

The story is good, when there is one.  Basically a comet crashed on the planet, created a plague that wiped millions out, mutating thousands, and humanity has had to mostly hide away to survive.  At the time of writing this, that hits a little too close to home.  What few humans aren't hidden away are either slaves or lambs to slaughter for the mutants who have created a dogmatic order on the world.  You hook up with the local resistance to very slowly step by step take back the town.  This part is amazing.  You actually feel like you're an important part of liberating the people.  However, this is like the first fifth of the game.  After beating the boss and freeing the town, you find a plot device.  Your goal is now to travel the world and complete the plot device.  The whole resistance angle gets put on the backburner and it never really gets addressed again.  There's one story decision you can make, which is admittedly one more than I would have expected from a DOOM clone.  There's voice acting and it felt like it was a bunch of people from the dev team who cared A LOT about getting their lines right.  That means that the actual voices are quirky but the actual acting is great.  

Hey guess what the gameplay is like DOOM.  The gunplay is brutal, the enemies are varied, and the levels were designed with an etch-a-sketch.  These levels were better than DOOM's mostly because you can press tab and pull up the map for where you are.  There's an inventory system so you can stock up on items but more importantly extra health and armor.  [b] Disable auto-use health kits as soon as you start the game unless you want to be left at the final boss with low HP and 0 medical supplies [/b].  The guns pack some bite, but a lot of that is lost under the poor gunplay.  Most of the enemies you're going to be fighting are not on the same verticality as you, and the crosshair is a liar.  You're going to waste a lot of ammo trying to aim at the hover drones because you will whiff a lot.  Ammo comes and goes a lot so make sure you keep your eyes peeled for secrets.

Tech wise it's DOOM.  You could probably run this on a coffee maker.  It's been reworked to run on modern systems by Night Dive Studios (the saviors of retro PC gaming) but you might run into a crash here or there.  The fact that this is on the DOOM engine is a problem since the cardboard cutout character models is poison for depth perception (and you're gonna need to be able to gauge distance when you come across enemies that are only damageable by the weapon that drains your HP to use).  The art direction is probably the best I've seen in a video game in a LONG time.  It looks like a comic book from the 1980s come to life.  

So that's Strife.  A relic of a bygone age.  It's still a good game but you should know what you're getting yourself into before you buy it.

Final Words: "I won't tolerate that kind of depravity... not without my cut."

Good game, revolutionary for 1996. If you're interested in the history of first person shooters OR computer roleplaying games you owe it to yourself to give it a spin. 

This is a fully voice acted (well, important NPCs anyway) story driven FPS-RPG hybrid that came out 2 years before the first Half-Life, 3 years before System Shock 2 and 4 years before Deus Ex. It's a true hybrid without erring too far to the RPG side (like System Shock 1) or the FPS side (like HeXen). So you have Doom combat, an interesting story and a pleasing art style, this is the definition of a hidden gem.

BUT this game is not perfect. The sewer level early on and the last 1/4th of the game can be a bit of a slog, with an emphasis on resource management that can get in the way of anyone looking for fast and furious action. There are also a lot of frankly annoying hit scan enemies in the later part of the game, many of them on the ceiling. Which brings me to the big downside of the "Definitive Edition" in particular: the vertical aiming is kind of wonky. It's not game breaking but it's noticeable and can be frustrating when you're trying to conserve ammo. *However* this release does come with the WAD files to play the game (both the Veteran and original DOS edition) in GZDoom or some other Doom source port if this bothered you that much. 

But back to minor gripes about the original design- I love the first 2 Dooms and I'm not usually bothered by mazes in old FPSs, but I found myself getting very tired of them by the end of this one. To the point that I skipped the extra level Nightdive added for the Veteran Edition in fact. The levels themselves are well designed, I think my fatigue came from a combination of two things. I've played both this game and the ZDoom port of the original.  Besides a few new maps, the Veteran Edition doesn't add a whole lot to what you get from the port in terms of gameplay.  It also throws in achievements, trading cards, and a couple of new in-game things (Blackbird chiding the player upon death or quiting; three collectible artifacts).  

Strife is an old-school shooter; it's built on the Doom engine.  It's not a game that holds your hand, though it doesn't throw you out on the street, either.  Several levels are very maze-like and can give inexperienced players problems.  Also, it's not always clear whether it's a good idea to head to an optional area once it's available or progress in the main story first.  I haven't tested it, but it's possible to render the game unwinnable if certain missions are done in the wrong order (I do know that the Veteran Edition removes one specific way of making it unwinnable).  

The levels are interconnected; with very few exceptions, it's possible to revisit every place you've been whenever you want.  Teleporters make travel a bit easier.  

The weapons in the game have a nice variety, though the electric bolts are pretty much completely worthless.  It's also quite easy to play through the game and never pick up the Mauler.  In my three playthroughs, I only grabbed it once. It's available in two or three places.  

The story is strong, with maybe two-dozen voiced characters.  However, the pacing is a bit odd.  Without giving anything away, this game ends rather abruptly.  After accomplishing a key task, you stroll into a structure which you didn't know existed before, fight through a couple of rooms of enemies, confront the final boss, and that's it.  The time between the penultimate task and the boss is five to ten minutes.  

If playing on harder difficulties, this game can be unforgiving.  It's not that the enemies are mercilessly hard (they're tough, but with only a couple exceptions are not overpowered); rather, it's that the health and ammo which you depend upon are available inconsistently.  It's very easy to find yourself low on supplies and in a tough spot.  Sometimes they're scarce; sometimes there's more than you can carry, forcing you to leave them behind.  You could theoretically backtrack and pick them up again when you need them.  

Strife is a rare example of an FPS/RPG hybrid.  The aforementioned voiced characters are a big part of it.  You can choose text responses in dialogue.  You don't make too many plot altering decisions, though several of them affect what order you perform your tasks.  It's also possible to miss large portions of the game, either through decisions or just not going to certain places.  

Overall, Strife is a very good game.  It has challenge and charm.  If you like old shooters, play this one.
Good game with an interesting story.  If you want something similar to Doom with some added spice then this is a great pick.

[h1][b]Long story short:[/b] An extremely obscure gem, mixing shooter and pseudo-RPG mechanics into a perfect blend. Though very difficult, if you like games such as System Shock 2 or Deus Ex, Strife is an excellent example of the genre fusion well before anything else was done. And it's worth picking up if you like retro shooters in general.[/h1]

I love Strife. I love the engine, the overworld, the shooting, the secrets, everything. It's one of those games that just reeks of originality and ingenuity that it's hard to even come to grips with the fact that it disappeared off the face of the planet shortly after it was released. The Veteran Edition, led by Night Dive Studios, is not only a faithful port of the original game, but also offers a re-done version that fixes up a lot of bugs, adds an unfinished game mode to it, and makes the Doom engine look brand spanking new. And it's glorious.

Strife came out in 1996, a month before Quake was released. Graphically, it definitely was overshadowed by Quake. The Doom engine could pull off some amazingly large locations and have tonnes of enemies on screen, but Quake was in full 3D, and it looked amazing (and also the level design was ridiculously good too). Strife faded into obscurity as Quake basically became the hall-mark for FPS standards.

Strife is mostly a first-person shooter: you move around, shoot bad guys, and walk around a map completing objectives. It had an inventory system similar to Heretic or Hexen before it, where health packs and other gadgets could be used. It had a bunch of weapons that could be used, and, in the retro shooter fashion, were completely explosive and amazing. My favourite has to be the grenade launcher, which fires two giant bombs forward, which explode into a tower of fiery death. There's also a secondary ammo for that weapon which fires napalm, and man is it devastating.

However, it also had a few RPG mechanics thrown in. Firstly, the entire game was a persistent overworld: you start in a main hub, and every level branches off from that, interacting with each other as the game goes on. Military bases become overrun, pathways open up between areas, and so on. You can also talk to almost every human character in the game. While a lot of them don't say anything useful, a few give some nice tips on fighting enemies or navigating the levels. Quite a number of NPCs are voice acted, and it definitely brings the game some life.

On top of that, levels have a lot of secrets involved with them. With the Veteran Edition, there are 16 that are marked and count towards an achievement (which honestly is not that many), but there are definitely a lot of other hidden away areas that include items, rewarding the player for keeping an eye out for inconsistencies in the level. One kind of secret actually increases your maximum health and makes your weapons more accurate, which is a nice way to reward the player rather than giving a bunch of ammo.

The story will leads you around a bunch of locations around the world. While it gives the illusion of an open-world game, it's really linear, as you're expected to clear off levels in a specific order. However, quite a few areas allow the player to approach it from different angles, similar to Deus Ex. For a lot of levels, stealth is an option. While the player, in a few areas, can walk around without guards attacking, robots will always hunt the player down, so stealth is more about avoiding enemies than trying to take out each of them one at a time. When stealth goes, the game doesn't make you feel like you've messed up, as your weapons are more than capable of taking down enemies (although on higher difficulties the number of enemies gets ridiculous). A few areas in the game do get quite ridiculous though in terms of irritating enemy placement or level design, but overall there's a lot of good stuff.

A lot of the enemies attack with hitscan-like weapons (or projectiles that move very fast). This can get a bit annoying and can contribute to a lot of deaths in the game. Again, fortunately in the Veteran Edition, a little blip comes up on the screen indicating where you are getting hit from, which makes it easier to react to them. Because of these enemies, your playstyle will move towards a more cautionary stance rather than running in rooms guns blazing. It's an interesting change of pace, but it does get a bit annoying when you die very quickly. Fortunately, hitscanning enemies are also the weaker enemies in the grand scheme of things (akin to Doom), which makes it not as cheap as it could be.

The story has you up against a few bosses, each one harder than the last. They also require to be hit with the ultimate weapon of the game: the Sigil, which upgrades its damage output and attack style after each boss is defeated. The Sigil uses the player's health as ammo, and it provides an interesting dynamic for the fights: where survivability is more crucial than before.

Strife also has a couple of different endings, and, fortunately, it isn't just a different button at the end of the final room of the game. The endings are determined in the last third of the game, and it changes the course of where you go and such. It's interesting to see a game from almost 20 years ago do this and many other elements so well compared to more modern games.

The Veteran Edition release not only fixes the original game's bugs, but it also offers the original game as a bonus which is nice. It also uses a fancy OpenGL version of the Chocolate Strife port, which offers bloom and dynamic lighting, but, again, there is an option to use the software renderer and make the game look as old as it originally did. Also the multiplayer is nice and chaotic as most retro shooters seemed to be. However, the player-base is not quite there yet, so it's hard to get into a match.

However, of course, the game not only includes support for modding, but it's compatible with a bunch of mods that were made back in 1996. While not as extensive as some other games at the time, there's a lot of good stuff that came out of the modding community back then, which will definitely extend the game's life cycle.

If you play Strife, you have to remember that it came out in 1996: well before any other shooter RPG hybrid that was big and popular. And it's sad just how amazing this game was. The Veteran Edition release is very faithful in making the game run well on modern systems, as well as making it compatible with older content. The $10 price point is well worth the content. Strife is a magnificent game, and you'll definitely like it if you're into retro shooters or shooter-RPG hybrids in general, or if you just want to play a hard as nails old school game.

After struggling through a string of bad games this was a refreshing one. I was a bit hesitant because I like modern FPS, I like late 90 FPS like Unreal or Half-Life but early 90s it starts to lose me. Doom was fun but I wasn't wild about it, Wolfenstein 3D I didn't enjoy, though Chex Quest, Rise of the Triad, and Dark Forces are fun. So where did this fall?

Despite being an older, non3d engine, this felt like a 3d game. Mouse moves freely, the game's length is about perfect. No map made some levels like the sewers feel annoying but these levels are all fairly small so easy to navigate. Fully voiced important npcs was nice. The weapons were all fun, though the 'shotgun' is treated as a end game weapon and I'd much rather have had a shotgun than the grenade launcher which was very encounter-specific due to bad range. The sprites at a higher elevation were immune to weapons besides the rifle or crossbow-- I had a few times where I shot a bazooka at a flying enemy to have it instead auto correct to blow up a civilian.  There's secret passageways that connect all levels together, had it been a modern game it'd be a open world. There was minimal platforming and what it did have was fun, I think that was a product of its game engine. It just didn't do platforming well and the game's devs were well-aware of the limitations of the game engine. 

Overall, I feel like Strife is a game  that was made too early. It's got all the hallmarks of a modern great FPS. Had it been made 10 or 20 years later it would have been known as a great game like Bioshock or FEAR. Instead when people think of great 90s FPS, including the ones I listed above and System Shock or Marathon, no one really thinks of Strife, and I think that's a shame. It lacks memorable enemies like Nazis, demons, or monsters that say Rise of the Triad, Doom, or Serious Sam used. But it has a fun story and worth checking out.

Important notes before I start the review: for the best experience, select the high quality render mode (unless you're a REAL retro freak). Other than that, pretty much nothing else. Let's get started. 

Strife is a classic Doom Engine FPS game set in a medieval world where a meteorite crashed on Earth, causing mutations in much of humanity. Some mutations caused rapid death and decay, others caused heightened intelligence and a strange spiritual connection to a mysterious entity. Those who mutated in such a way became The Order, a militaristic totalitarian government oppressing the common people and also building advanced technology such as robots, cyborgs, guns etc. You are a fighter for a resistance group known as The Front, with the job of infiltrating key Order territories as well as taking out their leadership with the help of a decent arsenal of weapons ranging from a machine gun to a flamethrower. While doing this, you are messaged by a mysterious woman called Blackbird. Sounds pretty crazy, doesn't it? Well, let me briefly talk about some mechanics. 

Strife, unlike other Doom Engine games from its time, has RPG elements. For instance, you can collect gold throughout the game and buy things such as ammo, armour, health kits etc. Another RPG element is stat upgrades. After completing a mission, you can go to the arms training room in the Front's base and increase your accuracy level. You can also go to the medic and receive implants that increase agility and maximum health. One more example of RPG elements is alternate endings. Depending on your actions, you can get 1 of 3 endings, each one with a wildly different outcome. The fact that the devs made a "Doom clone" with these features back in 1996 is honestly pretty amazing. They clearly wanted this to be a unique game and I'd say they succeeded. A few other great things that Strife has include good weapon variety, lots of brutal gore, decent voice acting (for the most part), brilliant comic book style art, challenging enemies (e.g. Crusaders, Templars etc.), and a fantastic soundtrack.

As much as I like this game, it does have its problems. One negative I can think of when it comes to Strife is that I found the level design to be quite confusing at times, leading to me being sometimes more frustrated than entertained. Also, despite v-sync being on, there were some textures in the game that would still have an odd screen tearing effect, which was a little distracting. Another thing that I hated was the fact that projectile weapons would sometimes not shoot in the direction I was pointing in, even if I had my accuracy stats upgraded. One more negative I should add is that Steam overlay doesn't work very well with this game. Sometimes I couldn't take screenshots and trying to turn the overlay on could take a long time. Oh, one more thing is that the multiplayer mode is completely dead. But these negatives are pretty minor overall. 

To conclude, Strife is a wonderful, underappreciated game and the Veteran Edition makes it run on modern hardware pretty much without flaw. The negatives I have are some choppy textures, occasionally confusing level design, shoddy aiming with projectile weapons, a dead multiplayer mode, and bad Steam overlay performance while playing. 

Final verdict: 7.5/10 "Get back to work, now!"

i first heard of this game from ross's game dungeon close to a decade ago, and i've been meaning to play it ever since. sometimes i would pick it up, play for half an hour, forget i even started it, lose time in some other game, then a year or 2 later come back and do the same thing, rinse repeat like 3-4 times, always interested, but never committed. until now, that is, as i'm going through my backlog in release order.
and for some reason, once i started playing this time, i was entranced by this game from the start and couldnt put it down.
see now, this is no simple 90s fps on the doom engine, this game decides to take doom and turn it into a story-based role-playing game. prior to this game, almost every first person shooter was pretty much "go through the maze killing every monster you see and humping the wall, find 3 keycards, get to the elevator", and theres nothing wrong with that, duke3d and blood are some of my favorite games of all time, but the genre needed something added to it, lest it stagnate. so now, you go from that, to this game that has a story, it has cutscenes with cool comic type art, you can talk to characters and they're voice acted with passion, you can take on quests and even side quests, there's a primitive wanted system, currency, shops, items that arent just guns or health, a massive map that doesn't just feel like levels but rather a world, hell you can even go back to other areas at almost any time,, you can level up your aiming and health, there are multiple endings, you have a woman talking in your head, you can even fight alongside and summon soldiers, this game is such an advancement from doom, it's insane.
but i am overhyping the rpg elements to this game, it's rather light on them actually. this is no daggerfall. you don't create a character, or fit him with gear (armor works like it does in doom, so i won't count that). there are so few side quests in the game, and they don't even amount to much, its usually just "get this chalice, ok go here for your reward.", leveling up isn't based on experience, but rather a reward for beating a mission, and only affects aiming and health (maybe also punch strength? i noticed i could gib basic enemies almost instantly later in the game). point is, the rpg elements are minimal. if you want a more proper rpg fps hybrid, well there's system shock. i guess ultima underworld and elder scrolls arena as well if you remove the shooter part. but all those games are rather... clunky.
this game, is not an fps-rpg hybrid. at most, it's an fps with rpg inspiration
however, what we really have here is a co-creator of the immersive sim genre, a major leap from system shock or ultima, where menus and general clunkiness could take you out of the experience, strife just controls like doom, but where doom had a level-based structure and didn't have (almost) any story, strife keeps you going through its world organically as the story drives you. half-life and system shock may be lorded as the granddaddies of imsims, but i'd say strife is the biggest, most important leap for the genre, and i can't recommend it to old school fps fans enough

Strife is a game that was mostly forgotten during its time, largely due to releasing just a month before Quake, so most people today aren't even aware of what it is.  Strife is a game made on id Tech 1, but it does a lot of interesting things with it that you wouldn't expect to see from the same engine that powered Doom. Strife has more of an RPG atmosphere, and features a persistent semi-open world with stores to shop at, people to talk to, voice acted dialogue, and even a few side quests. There are slight stealth elements, and though it goes more by the old rules of "it's still stealth as long as nobody's alive to sound the alarm" than any particularly fleshed-out system, a few of the game's missions can be played pretty differently by utilizing it. It's not a particularly in-depth RPG, mind you - the only stats you have are health and accuracy, and both are only increased at set moments instead of having any sort of XP system, the world isn't particularly large, and the story is generally pretty linear, outside of 3 or 4 optional levels and side quests, and most of the actual mission levels play more like standard Doom than any sort of RPG, but it's still an interesting take on the Doom formula.

 This particular version includes a few new things that weren't in the original, like a set of talismans that can be found in secret areas and a full new side-level to fight through with a new side quest to go along with it. The veteran edition is generally pretty well-made, but I did have a lot of problems with the vertical auto-aim; with it on, certain weapons like the rocket launcher tend to have a lot of trouble hitting enemies placed higher than you, but with it off I found other weapons like the assault rifle having strange accuracy issues, forcing me to aim about an inch below enemies to actually hit them. Overall, Strife isn't necessarily an amazing game, and the level design can be a bit dull at times, but it's still a pretty fun overlooked game that's interesting to see at the very least, if only to see the unique things they managed to do with the RPG functions.

Strife: Veteran Edition, developed by Rogue Entertainment and published by Nightdive Studios, is a modernized re-release of the groundbreaking 1996 first-person shooter Strife. As the last commercial game built on the Doom engine, Strife was ahead of its time in merging traditional FPS mechanics with role-playing elements, creating a unique hybrid experience that distinguished it from its contemporaries. The Veteran Edition, released in 2014, updates the game for modern systems with high-resolution support, widescreen compatibility, improved lighting, and Steam integration, including achievements and trading cards, while preserving the core gameplay and narrative that earned the original its cult following.

The game’s story is set in a dystopian future controlled by a fanatical religious organization known as “The Order.” Players take on the role of a mercenary who joins a resistance movement to overthrow the oppressive regime. Unlike many FPS games of its era, Strife places a significant emphasis on narrative and world-building. Players interact with a wide array of NPCs, gather information, and complete quests, creating a sense of agency and immersion that blends storytelling with action. This integration of narrative into a first-person shooter format was innovative for the mid-1990s and remains one of the game’s most compelling features.

Gameplay in Strife: Veteran Edition emphasizes exploration and player choice within its interconnected level design. While combat remains fast-paced and engaging, with a variety of weapons and enemy types, the game encourages players to approach objectives in multiple ways. Although the RPG elements, such as branching paths and player decisions, are not as fully developed as in later titles, the combination of exploration, interaction, and action creates a layered experience that rewards curiosity and experimentation. The Veteran Edition preserves these elements while smoothing technical limitations of the original, offering a more polished experience.

Visually, Strife retains its classic pixel-art aesthetic, which evokes a sense of nostalgia while effectively conveying its dystopian setting. The environments, though limited by the original engine, are carefully designed to provide variety and atmosphere, from industrial complexes to desolate wastelands. The soundtrack and ambient sounds contribute to the immersive mood, heightening tension during combat and adding weight to quieter narrative moments. Limited voice acting adds personality to key characters, further enhancing the storytelling and helping the game feel more dynamic despite its dated graphics.

The legacy of Strife lies in its ambitious genre-blending approach. By integrating RPG elements into an FPS framework, it paved the way for future hybrids like Deus Ex and influenced the evolution of narrative-driven shooters. The Veteran Edition not only preserves this legacy but also makes it accessible to modern players, allowing a new generation to experience the innovation and charm of the original game. While some aspects, such as the depth of RPG mechanics, feel dated compared to contemporary standards, the game’s core design, story, and atmosphere remain engaging.

In summary, Strife: Veteran Edition is a noteworthy example of genre innovation, combining first-person shooting with role-playing mechanics and a strong narrative focus. Its dystopian world, memorable characters, and mix of exploration and action provide a rich and historically significant experience. Though it may not fully realize all the potential of its hybrid design, it remains a fascinating and entertaining journey for players interested in the roots of narrative-driven shooters and the evolution of interactive storytelling.

Strife is an old-school FPS, made with the Doom engine, that never got much recognition, because it was a bit aged by the time of it's release and, even worse, it came out a mere month before Quake made shooters full 3D, making Strife look downright antiquated in comparison. It's a shame, because it's not only a very good game, it was downright revolutionary.

It was one of the first shooters to actually have an actual story in the game, instead of being just a mindless slaughterfest, before Half-Life made story in shooters normal. And Strife's plot is actually quite good, at least for its time. The story of the order and its underlying secrets is not really anything special, but it's interesting and, along with the gameplay, can keep you motivated for quite some time. It also uses a twist that would look rather bad or out-of-place in many other games, but works here very well and is foreshadowed enough. On the other hand, the plot can also get confusing and it's not always what exactly happened. It feels like the devs didn't think out the story quite as well, as they should have.

The characters are... serviceable. Non gets much screentime and development and they only exist to drive the plot forward. The most interesting one is your invisible companion Blackbird, who is quite chatty and lets out many entertaining comments, that sometimes skirt the fourth wall.

As with any old FPS, the gameplay is the most important part and even Strife is no exception. And as with any old FPS, it's no walk in the park. The enemies take away your health pretty quickly and if you have no healing items (or turned auto-heal off), you can find yourself dead very quickly. On the other hand, healing items are pretty plentiful, so the game isn't too harsh. At least on low-mid difficulties.

There are also light stealth elements, for which you have two "silent" weapons. Very light, though, since it's impossible to finish any area without combat (with on possible exception). For the most part, the purpose is solely to thin out the enemy ranks before the proper fight starts. Other enemies don't care if their companions die near them, expect when they are very close, so that works very well.

At first, it might look like the game is pretty free, not exactly open-world, but possibly non-linear. This is not the case, though. There is not much you can do aside from your current objectives and attempting to deviate from it can potentially make the game unwinnable (although the Veteran Edition makes it more fair in that regard). There is only one time where you can make a choice that affects the story, but even then there is clearly a "good" and a "bad" choice.

There are three endings. Two depend on the aforementioned choice, the last on whether you die in the final battle.

There are a good amount of weapons in the game and everyone is quite useful in their own right. Two weapons have alternative ammo and another one has an alternative fire mode, effectively increasing the amount of weapons. Also, one is modular and fires differently, depending on how many pieces you have. However, it also uses your health as ammo, so it's use is limited (mostly to enemies that can only be hurt by it).

The presentation is pretty much what one would expect from a 90's shooter in the Doom engine. It's 2.D, 3D but with 2D sprites for characters, items, decorations and pretty much everything that isn't the map itself and very pixelated. The music is MIDI only, which is a rather mixed thing. The songs itself are good, though. Important (and a few not so important) NPCs are presented with big portraits in a comic style, which are pretty well-done. They are also voiced, which is a mixed bag. Generally, the voice acting isn't very good, but the way it tends to be overdone and hammy is actually pretty entertaining. The best one is the aforementioned Blackbird, who has a pretty pleasing voice. Which is good, because you'll hear it the entire time.

The Veteran Edition improves the visuals with widescreen support and additional effects. Especially Bloom enhances the graphics a lot and makes it kinda hard to go back to "vanilla" Strife.

I can recommend this game to everyone who likes first-person shooters, especially old ones. By now, it doesn't look very impressive anymore, but it still holds up nicely and is especially interesting for retro shooter fans.

Strife can be confusing, janky and at times really test your patience- As all good boomer shooters should.

Massively different from most Doom Engine games, Strife almost feels like a modern day WAD, leaning into some light RPG elements and presenting the player with a decently sized and surprisingly immersive open world; there's town hubs, secret bases, shops to spend your gold at in between missions, side quests and even a very simple progression system that allows you to increase weapon accuracy, health and melee damage. 

None of this detracts from the tight, responsive game play you'll probably be familiar with if you've dabbled with boomer shooters; the weapons are deadly (as much to yourself as the enemy) and satisfying to use in spite of how...Quirky some of them behave and there's a nice variety of enemies that ramp up the combat as the game progresses, offering a nice mix of fast paced, frenetic encounters as well as some slower, more methodical areas to push through.

Is there actually stealth? Eh, sort of; there're two weapons in the game that don't set of alarms and there's even an achievement for completing a certain objective without setting of the area alarm, you can clear some of the humanoid enemies in an area before going in guns blazing for a slight edge, but robotic enemies are always hostile regardless and many areas feature "Alarm gates" which you have to pass through, by no means is this a stealth game but having the option to prepare an attach and set up a better approach is an interesting addition, even if it's not utilised all that much.

There's even an additional level and three powerful talismans to find in the Veteran Edition that weren't present on release, as well as some enhanced visuals which do look nice, but I personally disabled these options in favour of a chunkier, more pixelated aesthetic.

TLDR: Is it good? Yeh, it's a solid shooter that's satisfying to play, has an interesting 90's as all fuck story and world building, and might be a nice novelty for you if you haven't played it before but are a fan of the genre.

First of all, I really want to congratulate Night Dive. They've smoothed out many  of the rough elements of the original Strife, added some useful/cool new features, and generally done a great job at making Strife look and play better without really touching the game itself.

Here's a few of the improvements:

[list]
[*]High-resolution 3D-accelerated rendering engine with tweakable settings for pretty much everything. I think the bloom filter defaults are pretty good, but whatever your preference is, you can set it. You can even select the original software renderer if you want the old Doom engine look.
[*]Important quest items are now highlighted with a flashing outline when enemies drop them.
[*]Major mission objectives now have waypoints marked on the map screen.
[*]I've only tested controller support with a wired Xbox 360 controller, but man does it work well.
[*]An unused UI element for the secondary fire mode of the Mauler has been implemented. This makes the immediate distinction between fire modes a lot clearer.
[*]The original soundtrack can be played back in either a tinny-but-classic FM-chip version, or a superior pre-recorded MIDI version using good instrument samples.
[/list]

As for the game itself, Strife is a FPS/RPG hybrid with a heavy leaning towards the former. The FPS elements are interesting in that several of the weapons can hurt you if you're not careful - especially the grenade launcher and secondary fire mode of the Mauler. If you learn to use the weapons effectively, however, they can make you feel like a total badass. You cannot stealth through the whole game, but many areas allow you to get through with minimal killing if you'd like, and one achievement is based around doing this in a specific area.

The plot involves a couple of twists that you may or may not see coming. There's a couple of major areas that only open up if you take the path to the "Good" ending, and one or two that you can just simply miss by not exploring the levels enough.

The RPG elements of Strife involve branching NPC dialogue trees, (optional) upgrades to accuracy and health, and 3 different endings. This is nothing special today, but at the time, nobody had put all those features into a FPS, let alone a Doom engine game. The spoken dialogue is variable in quality - some characters are believable, others a little over-the-top. Thankfully, it's all way above the quality of many other old-school games.

You have essentially a running commentary from Blackbird (a female NPC who talks to you via your comm unit) throughout most of the game. It's a great idea that often helps to give the game some personality, as well as a reminder of where you need to go next.

Then, there's the secrets. Holy heck are there a lot of secrets in this game. I discovered a few secret areas here and there in my original playthroughs, and was pretty satisfied with myself. When I went about trying to get the "Completionist" achievement in this version, I noticed that many of the secrets I knew didn't even count towards the total. I'm now pretty humbled. To be fair, some of the secrets are not at all obvious, and some basically require bumping into/trying to open every square inch of every level [(The transparent wall secrets are some of the worst offenders in this category)]. Also, Night Dive *added* some secrets to this version of Strife, most notably the Talismans (which are a seperate accheivement). I'm currently running through the game specifically trying to find every secret without consulting a walkthrough. It's not easy.

Okay, so there's also some stuff that doesn't hold up so well:

Blackbird often comments on NPC dialogue - but sometimes she doesn't start talking until at least a second after the NPC's line has finished. If you're used to rushing through dialogue trees, you might miss about half of her lines. I can't remember if this was in the original game or not, but in this version a line of text will show up in the saying "Blackbird is listening", which lets you know she's going to comment after the NPC finishes talking.

The graphics are kind of blocky. This version has done a nice job of subtly filtering textures once they get a certain distance from the player, but this is still a Doom engine game. Thankfully, the overall art design is colorful and far from the bland color schemes of more recent FPSs.

The music is variable in quality, with some tunes adding to the intensity of combat [spoiler] especially the castle assault[/spoiler], and some becoming incredible repetitive after a while; the music in the sewer levels is especially grating (pun not intended).

While the lack of handholding in finding mission objectives is a nice change from modern games, there are some levels where it's very easy to get lost and not know what to do/where to go next. The objective waypoints on the map screen are a nice addition, but the markers are totally static and don't clear when individual objectives are achieved.

The multiplayer is limited to your Steam friends. This is great if you have several friends who like to play Strife, but it would be nice to have the option to play with strangers as well. Yes, I do also understand that dedicated servers are expensive to run.

Overall, this is easily the best "re-release with enhancements" I've played, and really helps to show folks what a cool, underappreciated gem Strife was/is.

A very distinct Doom engine game. It's pretty good.

Now, first thing that makes it so distinct is the fact it's a sort-of RPG. A pretty simple though, think like Stalker without side quests and random AI skirmishes. There's no leveling up beyond free upgrades that raise accuracy or hp you can get once in a while, there's money but they're only spent on ammo and consumable items, there's some free travel and location revisiting but movement is still tied to storyline and there's no proper sidequests to discover - although there's a single binary choice in the story, which affects the ending.

So, seeing how the RPG elements are pretty undeveloped, they really don't deserve as much attention as the FPS aspects - which is pretty comparable to Doom in pace, you run and shoot fast but sometimes you may get stuck navigating the mazelike level design, but a lot of weapons are somewhat more tricky, like there's grenade launchers it's easy to get killed with and there's an alt-fire mode that sets area on fire which is even easier to get killed with, there's an energy shotgun that may be tricky to use in combat due to firing delay, flamethrower sets enemies on fire and they can damage you by getting too close. Still, most of this damage can be mitigating by sensible gun use and avoiding damage when appropriate so it just makes the combat more interesting - on other hand, a lot of weapons are quite underwhelming - like the basic knife and crossbow are trash, even though the crossbow later gets a biological enemy instakill ammo type which may be pretty handy, flamethrower projectile is a bit slow while range is small which means you're likely to get damaged before enemies go up in flames, energy shotgun is also clumsy and wasteful, the always handy SMG got a modest ammo supply, and the final Sigil superweapon, while crucial to the plot and only thing able to beat the bosses, drains your life so you have to either constantly use up medikits from inventory not to get killed - and there's no "economy" alt fire mode, the more bits of the artifact you pick up over game the more it takes and the more it deals. Talking about health kits, this game has some items you can pick up, mostly it will be health packs, but there's also common in Doom and Duke era powerups like stealth, temporary chemical damage immunity suits. Some like auto-targetter are more unusual but I'll be honest I never found any application for them. I found the use for the secret three totem upgrade though, the game has like three totems you can find in it's second half, collecting them all transforms the previously crappy melee punch into a super high damage, massive knockback attack which is worth it.

Now, what I really like about this game is the art direction and setting. It's a very unusual setting, a primitive, feudal world full of humans that one day gets hit by a comet that spreads a virus turning many of aflicted into fanatics - ruthlessly dedicated to some goal only they understand, yet also granted great knowledge about advanced technology, cybernetics, energy weapons. So you have a world of medieval peasants and castles where mechs, cyborgs and guns are commonplace. The sprites and textures are nice for their time but they're not as rad as the loading screen slideshow cinematics with narration, ones from intro and endings, those haven't aged one bit despite being pixely. The soundtrack is also great and memorable, even if some bits are more dull.

This is a great update of an interesting old game, if you're the sort of person to enjoy more unusual Doom .wads that add all sorts of new gimmicks to experience, you should also try this! Also if you like this I may suggest Wolfendoom Blade of Agony, a free standalone Doom mod that arguably does a lot of things in a very similar manner.

Strife may have been revolutionary in the early 90's, but it does not hold anything to modern FPS-RPG games.

30-something men will tell you that this game is the coolest, but really it is beyond nonsense. Placing you into a medieval dystopian setting, you are to use crossbows, missile launchers and machine guns to kill soldiers in metal armor. These medieval soldiers fire back at you with, get this, machine guns. You'll run across space blobs and robotic spiders, too. Head on down to "Ye Ol' Weapons Shop" to purchase crossbows and machine gun rounds, or try the armor store next door to buy metal armor so you too can make absolutely no sense, just like your enemies and surroundings.

This game isn't good by any rules today. I thought Wolfenstein was alright, and the old Duke Nukems were pretty good too. This game was just a failure in an attempt to put FPS into RPG elements. The RPG elements consist of randomly placed NPCs who give you incredibly vague (at least early on) quests. It's very easy to kill someone who could give you a huge quest if you don't talk to them first. On many characters, there are no graphics rendering them different than any other peasant, which means you will have to literally speak to every character on the map in order to find quests properly without a guide.

When you speak to these people, a pretty nice cartoon visual of their face will pop up, and then you will hear the voice acting. Oh god, the voice acting made me want to continue playing this game with how laughable it was. You'll walk through medieval times wielding your machine gun, and come upon a peasant with a brooklyn accent who's telling you to get to work before the guards shoot ya.

TL;DR - This game was revolutionary as the first FPS RPG, but revolutionary does not usually go hand-in-hand with good.  This game has poor quests, poor voice actors, and a clunky feel that makes it annoying. You can't disable headbob in this release, so the best way to play is to use GZDoom to launch this version, and then disable headbob in the console (~ key) by typing "movebob 0" (no quotes) and hitting enter.  Will save you motion sickness.

Can't disable weapon sway here either, but again you can in GZDoom... under options ---> display options, there is a slider for it.

FoV can be adjusted in this release.  In-game there is a slider that shows min and max values but doesn't show you what number it's specifically set to.  You can make more accurate adjustments to the FoV by navigating to the game's install folder, opening the chocolate-strife CFG file, and editting the number at the end of the "gl_fov" line.

The load times are even faster in GZDoom when playing Strife compared to the official Veteran release (instant compared to ~1 second due to a fade transition). You can also use number keys for dialogue inputs in the GZDoom version of this release, but in the official release, numbers aren't recognized in dialogue.  The menus are also higher res when using GZDoom as opposed to the official release.

Playing in GZDoom also gives the option of the (beta) Poly rendering, which *mostly* fixes the camera perspective so the game world doesn't alter size based on player viewpoint (ie. looking up or down without Poly rendering on causes the ceiling to come closer or the ground to come closer, depending on whether you're looking up or down).  This official update doesn't completely fix this, it still has remnants of the broken view perspective of the original, which admittedly all games that used this engine had until the unofficial engines came out to fix it.  To be fair, at time of writing the GZDoom optional method to fix this doesn't entirely rectify it either, but it's also still in Beta.

The only upside I can see for single-player when playing on the official engine vs. GZDoom is there are quest markers on the map when using the official release.  You're trading the ability to disable headbob and weaponsway, instant load times, and number keys for dialogue navigation, for quest markers.  Quest markers are definitely a plus, but with all the other unofficial features being absent, it still ends up making this difficult to recommend at the asking price.

There is a good reason for this: the further you get into the game, the less significant the elements I mentioned earlier which make the game unique really have any effect. By the end, it's just navigating maze-like levels looking for the right switch, mowing down masses of enemies that cross your path with your impressive aresenal of weapons. In other words, it gradually devolves into every other shooter of its time. 

Another issue I have is just how little variety there is. All the enemies - save one type - are either acolytes or robots. Most of the settings are either medieval-style castles or technological settings that could have been pulled out of a contemporary Star Wars game. There's a bit where you first leave town and find yourself in the outskirts, where it looks like you'll get a new kind of outdoor setting. 

I still enjoyed playing this game, and played it all the way until the end. But honestly, if you aren't someone who played it back in the day and wants to rekindle memories or whatever, I don't really see the point in playing this. It might be an interesting curiosity to see an extremely early example of an FPS incorporating these elements from other genres, I suppose, but you might find your interest waning the further in you get.

it's sort of interesting in its jank and what it attempted to do within its time period, especially under the conditions in which it was made to do them, but while its ambition gives it a charm it also gives it a whole bundle of problems that don't quite make for a very fun fps.

the open world is more confusing and empty in its nature, the writing isn't especially compelling or charming except in its early fps narrative jank, the level design is weaker than some of its counterparts with the respectable effort to construct things that should feel like real locations not quite matching up to the efforts of duke or blood while feeling even more like a mass of abstract confusing grey halls than doom or marathon. a few of the guns feel good--the flamethrower is very satisfying, and the grenade launcher while annoying to aim, feels great to render a room of enemies into pulp with, though the rocket launcher feels about the same as what you'd get in doom--but a lot of the enemy and boss design feels very bad.

strife is an interesting curiosity but as a game i didn't really have a great time playing it. many of its ideas are ones i enjoy a lot in other fps games, but the execution just isn't there in strife, its rpg mechanics are a rarely utilized side feature and it's hard to even call its stealth... stealth, given your lack of options and ways to stay concealed it largely amounts to a few sections where you can avoid starting a fire fight for about five minutes instead of five seconds. and once its novelty wears away it all depends on how you find its strength as a regular fps game of its time, which is an area where i find it pretty unsatisfying on the whole.

Nightdive does a great job of bringing old games to modern systems, their good work continues here with Strife.

When I was younger, I remember playing the demo for Strife fondly, and pining for the full release... playing it now, I'm sort of glad I never experienced it.

I think Strife is a good example of a game where the demo was better than the full release - thankfully that same demo is actually included.

The early openings of Strife are really promising - using your brain over mindless shooting, alarms, silently killing guards, talking to NPCs who have some great lines of spoken dialogue, optional quests, shops and an actual narrative - and this is pretty much the demo area... there is a lot going for Strife at the start of the game, but sadly by mid-game you're playing another generic boomer-shooter, rolling around and mindlessly shooting the same sort of enemies.

By the end game the levels become bland and unimaginative, large open areas with very little going on other than enemies to deal with and the odd boss fight.

I mean, hey, for a game released in 1996, it is good and ambitious - but for me, it doesn't hold up. It's neither here nor there. Strife is not different enough [from the likes of other shooters of the time] to make it a classic, sadly but fans of the genre should take a look.
